en: *The Direct Pointing to the Zen Source: A Family Treasure* (The Essential Method for Attaining Buddhahood and Becoming an Ancestor; Mind-Realization and Seeing [Gui] Must-Know).
Composed by Tianji of Yangzhou City.
Proofread and carved by his sons, Shanian and Songnian.

The secret transmission of the essential methods for practicing Chan meditation and the work of the Buddha-dharma requires, first and foremost, the establishment of a firm resolve. For resolve is the commander of the vital energy (*qi*).
If a person establishes a firm resolve, it is like commanding a million troops; with majestic power on all sides, one may pierce through the heavens and the sun—what task would not be accomplished?
It is accomplished thus. Generally, those who fear difficulties lack firm resolve; those who follow the flow of circumstances lack firm resolve;
those who change their minds upon hearing words and abandon the path midway lack firm resolve; and those whose diligence and indolence fluctuate from beginning to end all lack firm resolve.
I once composed the "Heart-Method for Reading Books," and at its very outset, I stated: "If one's resolve is firm, even what is difficult becomes easy. Now, regarding this...
This is the practice of the Buddha-dharma; it is also like this.
When one’s resolve is firm, the task will surely be accomplished. I shall now discuss this in terms of worldly affairs.

For example, there was the King of Yue in his revenge against the Wu enemy, Zhang Liang in his retribution for the grievance of the state of Han, and Di Renjie in his restoration of the Tang dynasty. Altogether—
Because one’s resolve is fixed, the undertaking is accomplished and the result corresponds to it; the Buddha-dharma is likewise so.
A popular proverb says: "A man without resolve is like dull iron lacking hardness; a woman without resolve is like rotten straw lacking pith."
Regarding the practice of the Buddha-dharma, this resolve is of the utmost importance.
As the Great Master Zhongfeng sang: "It is neither difficult nor easy; it simply requires that a man possess a true resolve."
One whose will is true possesses the four powers that are firm and strong. With such strength, advancing on the Path is like a game; this is the method for attaining realization.
In the practice of the Buddha-Dharma, everything depends entirely upon awakening. One must know that for an ordinary person, a single moment of awakening is itself a single moment of Buddhahood.
If a Buddha lacks even a single moment of awakening, that very moment makes him an ordinary person. This is because awakening is itself the Buddha, and the Buddha is itself awakening.
Whether one is a Buddha or an ordinary person depends solely on whether there is awakening or non-awakening.
When the human mind possesses awareness, it is itself Buddha. It can open the gateway of practice for the Six Perfections and cross the ocean of kalpas of the three *asaṃkhyeya* aeons.

Universally benefiting beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, its vastness resides in merit and wisdom. Attaining the six kinds of supernatural powers, one perfects the fruit of Buddhahood in a single lifetime.
Even the fiery cauldrons and icy rivers, upon hearing [this teaching], are transformed into fragrant groves; those who drink molten copper or enter the iron [hells] are likewise [liberated].
Then all shall be born in the Pure Land.
Regarding the practice of the Buddha-dharma, I have a wondrous secret formula consisting of a single phrase—just four characters: "Firmly maintain right awakening.
One must understand that "the power of faith becomes daily firmer" means it is steadfast and no longer changes; "the power of mindfulness becomes daily maintained" means one holds fast to it.
One does not weary of its duration. Perfect Enlightenment (Sambodhi) is perfectly luminous and universally illuminating; it is neither partial nor deficient.
If a person can give rise to this Perfect Enlightenment, their original nature will naturally manifest. All deluded minds will be subdued of themselves, without waiting for them to be expelled.
It is like the light of the sun: once it shines, all darkness is dispelled into clarity. Although these words consist of only four characters, [they encompass the entire meaning].
In truth, there is only this single word "awakening" (jue). However, this awakening is achieved entirely through concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā).

One need not fear the arising of thoughts; one only fears awakening too late. To awaken as soon as a thought arises, and for that thought to vanish upon awakening—this is the sublime method of cultivation.
It is like knowing that one is dreaming; then one will no longer be deluded.

If a person can attain this awakening, they must rouse their spirit; it is like a general on the battlefield or a judicial official in court—there must not be even a hair’s breadth of dullness or drowsiness.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one must be firm in resolve and possess constancy.
If one lacks constancy, one will often abandon the path midway or cease upon achieving only slight progress; these are all instances of self-abandonment, which is deeply regrettable.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, the greatest fear is interruption. If one practices diligently for a month, one may have already reached the highest vehicle;

yet if one interrupts for only ten or fifteen days, that superior attainment will be lost to where it went. Furthermore, one must not rely on the diligence of the previous month as a basis for self-conceit.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one most fears dullness and distraction.
However, this dullness and distraction are entirely caused by one’s own lack of firm resolve and lack of sincere faith in the Way; it is truly a great pity.
The practice of the Buddha-dharma requires entirely self-investigation and self-awakening.
Even the most intimate relationships—such as those between father and son or teacher and friend—cannot substitute for this; nor can it be transmitted through the technical skills of worldly arts.
It is like when another person eats: only that other person’s belly is satisfied, while one’s own belly remains hungry. (Huisi Dashi)
The Master said: "The source of the Way is not far; the ocean of nature is not distant. Simply seek it within yourself; do not look for it elsewhere.
Even if you seek it, you will not find it; even if you were to find it, it would not be real. This is what is meant by 'seeking oneself is better than seeking others.'"
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, all twelve hours of the day and night are times for applying effort.
If you are willing to apply effort when waking at the fifth watch or rising early at dawn, your practice will increase twofold.

You must know that the early morning is the time when the qi of heaven and earth is most clear and fresh, making it the most suitable moment for drawing it inward; one must not pass this time by in negligence or idleness.

The practice of the Buddha-dharma does not consist merely in sleeping at the fifth watch and rising at the third; one must simply fear being warm for ten days after a single day of exposure to the sun.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one must recognize that there are many evil conditions in the mundane world, such as birth, old age, sickness, death, and sorrow.

Suffering and distress are called the bridle and the iron chain; amidst the startling winds and terrifying waves, even if one should experience a slight moment of joy, it is likewise a hollow flower without substance, lasting but a brief instant.
One must see through this with complete penetration before one knows that the Buddha-dharma is the means for rescuing oneself from the sea of suffering;
only then will one joyfully and gladly apply oneself to it.

Regarding the practice of the Buddha-dharma: if one approaches it with joyful enthusiasm, it will naturally become easy to apply effort, and one will naturally progress with diligence and without slackening.

This joyful enthusiasm must be cultivated by observing the various sufferings of others in this world—birth, old age, sickness, and death—as if they were one's own own failure to apply effort. How could one remain indifferent?

In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one most fears engaging in idle talk and meddling in others' affairs. You must know that idle words and idle matters cause the mind to disperse and the spirit to wander;
they are beneficial in nothing but harmful. Furthermore, they cause one’s precious time to be wasted in vain—truly a great pity.
Regarding the practice of the Buddha-dharma, if one exerts effort for too long, one cannot avoid becoming weary. It is necessary to walk about and relax;
by relaxing, one nourishes the spirit. Once the spirit is restored, return to your practice, and natural clarity and awakening will arise.
To be overly strenuous and stubborn—persisting in arduous toil not only dulls the nature and impairs its acuity, but also weakens the physical body.
When illness arises in a person, their spiritual practice comes to a halt. Though they do not wish for it to be slow, it inevitably becomes so.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one must exert diligence every single day;

if one remains negligent and complacent, even if one passes through hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes, there will never be a day of success. When people of old applied themselves to their work...
Light a stick of incense. When you see it burn out, reflect upon yourself, saying: "My practice remains as it was before, without any loss or gain.
How many sticks of incense pass in a single day? How many sticks in a year? Yet time passes all too easily; it does not wait for us.
The Great Matter is not yet clear—when will it be resolved? From this, feel deep regret and redouble your efforts.
Exert yourselves! Master Zhu Wen Gong of our Confucian school said: "Do not say that you will not study today, for there will be tomorrow;
do not say that you will not study this year, for there will be next year. The days and months pass away, yet the years do not wait for us.
Alas, one has grown old—who is to blame? The practice of the Buddha-dharma is likewise so. It is simply a matter of time.
To practice for two days is to achieve a lifetime's worth of merit; yet to merely wait for tomorrow for four days is to squander a lifetime.
The cultivation of the Buddha-dharma is exactly like this.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one must neither be lax nor overly hasty. It is like a skilled traveler who covers a hundred *li* each day;
by traveling only seventy or eighty *li*, one’s strength remains sufficient and the sinews do not grow weary.
If, however, one relies on one’s robust physical vigor and exceeds the distance of a hundred *li*—
Externally, one naturally runs about in haste and agitation until inevitably becoming exhausted; on the following day, one may even be unable to walk.
It is precisely because of this that practitioners of cultivation often fall ill.

Regarding the practice of the Buddha-dharma: if the body becomes weary and exhausted, one may apply force to the two shoulders by twisting them forward, backward, upward, and downward several dozen times.
Thus, the blood and qi throughout the entire body will circulate, the spirit will become refreshed and alert, and various ailments will not arise.
This is the "double-pivot" method of the practitioners of cultivation. It can also dispel all cold pathogenic influences.
Regarding the practice of the Buddha-dharma, some may ask: "One should simply take inquiry and realization as the primary focus; why must one also preserve the physical body?"
I say that this is to cultivate the Real by relying upon the provisional. It is like brewing tea:
if there were no fire from the stove, how could the tea brew itself? Should the stove break or the fire go out, the tea will inevitably grow cold.

Furthermore, such a method not only places excessive emphasis on ritual action, but also risks making the matter difficult to resolve, ultimately leading to wasted time and failure. Those of clear understanding will discern this.

Regarding the practice of the Buddha-dharma, it goes without saying that one must be diligent during the day and never be indolent. Whenever you apply yourself to practice at night, it should last only until the first watch;
it need not be prolonged. If a person does not sleep after midnight, the blood will not return to the liver, and illness may result from this in the future.
Furthermore, there is a certain class of people who can "refine away demons" and remain awake, which is quite extraordinary.
If one does not understand the practice of the Buddha-dharma, how could it depend on whether one is asleep or awake?
The practice of the Buddha-dharma can be applied during walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. Even when sitting for a long time, one may also engage in movement.
If one practices for a long time, what prevents sitting again? It is not that one must be exclusively devoted to sitting.

There was a student who practiced "sitting for long periods and not lying down," to which the Sixth Patriarch enlightened him, saying: "Since birth you have sat and not lain; after death you will lie and not sit.
This is but a set of stinking bones—why do you labor to perform such meritorious exercises? This clearly reveals the essential pivot of sitting and lying.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, it is most essential to give rise to a resolute mind determined to break through birth and death.

One must see through the world and one’s own body and mind as being merely provisional conditions without reality. If you do not awaken to the great matter that is inherently possessed, then the mind of birth and death will not be broken.
As long as the mind of birth and death is not broken, the demon of impermanence—the slayer—will ceaselessly strike at every thought-moment.
How, then, can one dispel this? Take this single thought as a tile for knocking at the door;
it is like sitting amidst a blazing fire, seeking an escape. One must not take a single step of distraction, nor can one remain stationary for a single moment.
At this moment, you must not entertain a single extraneous thought; you cannot hope for someone else to save you.
You must simply disregard the raging fire, disregard your own life, place no hope in being rescued by others, and give rise to no other thoughts.
Without even a moment’s hesitation, you must charge straight forward. Only if you manage to break through is one truly a hero.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one must affix the single character for "death" upon the forehead and treat this physical body of flesh and blood as if it were already dead.
One seeks only to investigate thoroughly this present moment of thought;
this very thought before one is like a long sword leaning against the sky—should anyone touch its edge, they would utterly perish. It is like polishing a dull blade until it is sharp.
If you are dull-witted, the sword has long since departed.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one most fears becoming attached to states of stillness; this causes people to become mired in arid desolation without realizing it.
One must understand that while people loathe states of movement, they rarely feel such aversion toward states of stillness. This is because worldly people have always remained amidst clamor.

In the midst of clamor, there is that which corresponds to a state of stillness; it is like eating molasses or honey, or like a person exhausted from long toil who delights in sleep, becoming naturally attached to it without even realizing it. One must urgently and swiftly recognize and break through this.
The teachings of external paths command the severance and extinction of body and mind, transforming them into withered wood and cold ashes; these too enter through the state of stillness.
If this continues for years and months, becoming ever more withered and ever more silent, one falls into a state of ignorance—how does this differ from being mere withered wood and cold ashes?
When practicing within the state of stillness, the sole requirement is to bring forth the thread of the robe.

The next section concerns the Great Matter. One might think that it can only be realized within a state of stillness; yet, when seeking the characteristic of stillness within this Great Matter, it is utterly unattainable.
It is attained precisely at the moment one attempts to attain it.

In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are essential. One must understand that concentration and wisdom are like the front and back of a single object;
they are two yet not two, and one cannot be separated from the other. However, when concentration arises, how can it be helped that dullness (*styāna-middha*) also arises along with it?
If dullness arises, concentration departs. When wisdom arises, how can it be helped that distraction (*vikṣepa*) also arises along with it?
If distraction arises, wisdom departs; I have a sublime Dharma for their regulation.
Only when concentration is clarified can concentration and wisdom achieve success; only when wisdom is tranquil can wisdom and concentration achieve success.
These two cannot be separated, nor can they be joined; merged into one, they reach completion.
How wondrous! To be able to know this Dharma—how could attaining the Way be difficult?
For a person to clarify the mind and see the nature to become a Buddha or a Patriarch depends solely on applying effort within concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

If one understands the wondrousness of concentration and wisdom, it is as easy as turning over one's hand; if one does not understand the wondrousness of concentration and wisdom, it is as difficult as ascending a mountain.
O Deva, whether it is difficult or easy depends entirely upon one's own capability.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is the essence of wisdom (*prajñā*), while wisdom is the function of concentration. It is like a lamp and its light: the lamp is the essence of the light.
Light is the function of the lamp; these two manifest one another and must not be weighted unevenly.

At the very moment of wisdom (*prajñā*), concentration (*samādhi*) is present within wisdom; at the very moment of concentration, wisdom is present within concentration. Although their names are two, their essence is fundamentally no different.
If there is concentration without wisdom, it immediately lapses into dullness (*styāna*); if there is wisdom without concentration, it immediately lapses into distraction (*vikṣepa*).
They must be cultivated in tandem; they must not be separated.

In my previous treatise, I have already explained in detail the methods for balancing concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Yet, fearing that there may still be points that remain unclear, [I shall speak further].
I shall now explain this once again. What I call "sinking" (styāna) is precisely what worldly people call "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
What I call "distraction" (vikṣepa) is precisely what worldly people call "erroneous conceptualization" (vikalpa).

One must understand that meditative concentration (samādhi) is generally the state of indeterminate mind over many lifetimes, while wisdom (prajñā) is generally the state of erroneous conceptualization over many lifetimes. Although concentration can treat erroneous conceptualization, it nevertheless...
It gives rise to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Although wisdom (*prajñā*) can counteract the indeterminate, it may still give rise to discursive thought (*vikalpa*).
In today’s practice, one must simply possess concentration (*samādhi*) informed by wisdom; one must never enter a state of drowsiness or indeterminate concentration.
One must simply possess wisdom supported by concentration; one must never enter a state of distracted or discursive wisdom. These two are not two; concentration and wisdom are fused.
Harmony is precisely where their merits converge.

The Great Master Zhi of Tiantai transmitted the sublime Dharma of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight). He taught that by practicing *śamatha* one observes, and through stillness one attains clarity;
this enables the moving mind to become still and the still mind to become clear. When there is clarity, there is illumination; when there is illumination, there is oneness. This—
This truly points to the path of awakening for all sentient beings; it is simply the method of fixed concentration and wisdom.
This is precisely the method of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* taught by the Great Master. Why, then, seek the Buddha-dharma elsewhere?

When a person is on the verge of departing this world, if they possess the merit of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they will certainly ascend to the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).

However, this wondrous Dharma depends entirely upon familiarization during one's ordinary days. The wise say: "If worldly people remain in a state of dullness and distraction all day long, how could they possibly attain concentration and wisdom at the moment of death?
If practitioners maintain concentration and wisdom all day long, how could they possibly fall into dullness and distraction at the moment of death? This being so...
To dig a well when one is already thirsty—how could this possibly suffice?
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, the most essential point is the word "earnestness" (qie). This word possesses immense power;
if one is not earnest, indolence will arise. Once indolence arises, one becomes negligent and unrestrained, leading to all manner of transgressions.
If one’s application of mind is sincere and earnest, how could negligence and indolence ever arise?

You should know that if you can internalize this single word "earnestness" (*qiè*), you need not worry that the resolve for liberation will not be shattered by the cycle of birth and death, nor need you worry that you will not reach the stage of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
To discard this word "earnestness" and seek the Buddha-dharma elsewhere is nothing but the deluded madness of non-Buddhist heretics.
The single word "intimate" (*qie*) is the most intimate expression. If one applies the mind with intimacy, there will be no gaps;

for this reason, various kinds of demons and devils cannot gain entry. If one applies the mind with intimacy, one naturally does not give rise to conceptual calculations or thoughts of existence and non-existence, and thus does not fall into the paths of externalists.
The single word "cut" (qie) not only eliminates faults; it immediately transcends the three natures of good, evil, and neutral.
When the mind is applied with great intensity to a single phrase of the *huatou*, one does not contemplate good; when the mind is applied with great intensity, one does not contemplate evil;
when the mind is applied with great intensity, one does not fall into the neutral. When the *huatou* is intense, there is no agitation; when the *huatou* is intense, there is no dullness.
Deeply settled. As soon as right awakening manifests before one, all demons naturally retreat. However, if awakening is not urgent, it will not arise.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one does not fear death but fails to attain life; rather, one fears life but fails to attain death.

If you can bind the state of doubt and the mind into a single place, then moving objects will dispel themselves without needing to be discarded, and the deluded mind will be purified without needing to be cleansed.
Thus, one is naturally purified. At the gateway of the six sense organs, there is spontaneously a state of vast openness; upon being pointed out, one arrives;
upon being called, one responds. How could one worry about not being alive?
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one must entirely maintain a state that is upright, firm, and unbending, remaining detached from worldly sentiments.

If one responds according to emotional impulses, then spiritual practice will not take root; moreover, if this continues for months and years, one will eventually conform to the common flow of worldly customs.
It is truly a pity. For example, when one has affairs of one's own, how can one find the leisure to manage the affairs of others?
To be central, upright, and resolute is itself *samyaksambodhi*.
Regarding the practice of the Buddha-dharma, the first requirement is right awakening (*samyag-bodhi*).
This right awakening consists in, at every moment, reflecting upon one's own luminous clarity (*prabhāsvara-citta*). One must not allow it to wander away.

If this luminous clarity wanders, one becomes like a corpse with breath, falling into dullness and thoughtlessness, descending into a state of stubborn emptiness and arid stillness. Even if one applies effort...
To exhaust oneself in laborious toil is of no benefit whatsoever.
As for the practice of the Buddha-Dharma, if one can truly apply oneself, it is like carrying a load of a thousand catties that one cannot set down even if one wishes;
it is like searching for a lost object of great importance—if it is not found, one vows never to cease the effort. Within this, however, one must simply avoid...
To give rise to grasping, to give rise to attachment, and to give rise to conceptualization: grasping becomes illness, attachment becomes a demon, and conceptualization becomes the external.
When one attains a single mind and a single intent—like searching for a lost object—then these three dissolve and cease to interfere with one another.
That which is called the arising of the mind and the movement of thought is itself the essence of the Dharma.
Regarding the practice of the Buddha-dharma: when raising up the *huatou*, one must remain vividly clear and alert, like a cat stalking a mouse.
As the ancients said, "If I do not slay Li Nu, I shall never rest. Otherwise, you will merely sit within a ghost cave.
In a state of drowsy stupor, one passes through a lifetime—what benefit is there in this?
When a cat catches a mouse, it opens its eyes wide and braces its four paws; it desires only to seize the mouse, and succeeds only when it reaches its mouth.
Even if there were chickens and dogs nearby, one would have no leisure to look back at them; the practice of Zen is just like this.
It is simply a matter of being resolute and intent on clarifying this principle. Even if the eight sensory objects are jumbled before one, one has no leisure to look back.
As soon as a stray thought arises, not only can the "rat" not be caught, but even the "cat" runs away.
In the practice of the Buddha-Dharma, one must not speculate upon or recklessly offer explanations regarding the public cases (gong'an) of former masters.
Even if you were to comprehend each and every word perfectly, it would have no connection to your own self.
You must realize that a single word or phrase from these predecessors is like a mass of blazing fire: it cannot be approached, nor can it be touched; how could you possibly sit or lie down within it?
Is it so? To further divide this into large and small portions, and to debate its superiority or inferiority—what benefit is there in this?
This matter does not accord with the scriptural vehicles (śāsana-yāna). Therefore, even those who have long practiced the Mahāyāna path do not know or recognize it;
how much less so for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the various Hīnayānas? Do the Three Worthies and Ten Sages not all thoroughly understand the teachings?
To speak of this single matter: the three vehicles tremble with dread, and those of the ten stages are struck with terror.

Even when Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment preach the Dharma like clouds and rain, delivering inconceivable numbers of sentient beings and entering the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they are still said to possess the "delusion regarding the knowable" (*jñeya-āvaraṇa-moha*).
This is already entirely contrary to the Way; how much more so for all others? Indeed, this matter begins from the stage of ordinary beings.
To suddenly identify with the Buddha-body is difficult for people to believe. Those who believe are vessels; those who do not believe are not vessels.

All practitioners who wish to enter this vehicle of the school must enter through faith. Within the single word "faith," there are degrees of shallowness and depth, as well as the false and the correct;
these must be distinguished. Regarding the shallow level, when anyone enters the gates of the Dharma, who would say they do not have faith? It is simply that they believe...
Regarding this Dharma gate: those who do not believe in their own minds—even the profound Mahāyāna bodhisattvas—do not yet possess full faith.
As the *Huayan shu* (Avataṃsaka Commentary) states: "To perceive one who can preach the Dharma and a multitude who listen to the Dharma is still not to have entered the gate of faith.
If it is said, "The mind itself is the Buddha," who would say they do not believe? Yet, when asked, "Are you the Buddha? then...

One stammers and tries to brush it aside, unable to take responsibility for it. The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Even if one exhausts all thought to measure it together, one cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
Why, then, does one have a mind that exhausts thought to measure? It is simply because faith is not complete.
Regarding the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox: that one's own mind is itself the Buddha is called "right faith. To seek dharmas outside the mind is called "heterodox.

Faith that [one's] mind is the Buddha requires one to investigate and clarify one's own mind through direct experience and practice, reaching a state of non-doubt; only then is it termed "right faith.
If one merely speculates in a state of confusion, saying "the mind is the Buddha" while actually failing to recognize one's own mind, this is termed "heterodox faith."
The former masters attained stability while picking and selecting; they attained stability while weeding the fields; they also attained stability while performing manual labor.

How could this be a case of sitting for a long time and forcibly suppressing [the mind] so that it does not arise, and only then considering it concentration? If it were like that, it would be called "perverse concentration" (mithyā-samādhi) and would not accord with the true intent of the Buddha-dharma.
The Sixth Patriarch said: "The nāga is always in samādhi; there is no time when it is not in samādhi. One must penetrate to see the fundamental essence before one can correspond with this samādhi.
Thus, Śākyamuni descended from Tuṣita Heaven, entered the royal palace, went into the Snowy Mountains, and beheld the morning star.
He opens the convention for the assembly. [The mind] has not yet emerged from this samādhi; were it otherwise, it would be swept away by moving objects. What then could be called "samādhi"?
One cannot find a place of arising within moving objects, nor can one find a place of arising within still objects.

Since the moving objects have no place of arising, what can be taken as their object? If you realize this meaning, you will see that it is all one single, fixed essence, pervasive and all-encompassing, with nothing remaining to be accumulated.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one must not be stained by worldly dharmas. Within the Buddha-dharma itself, one must not allow even a single speck of attachment;
how much more so with worldly dharmas? If the true *huatou* manifests before you, you will walk upon water without feeling cold and tread upon fire without feeling heat.
You will pass straight through a thicket of thorns with your body stretched out, seeing no obstruction. Only then can you abide within worldly dharmas.
In the midst of it, one must strike straight through horizontally; otherwise, one will merely break through objective conditions and turn away from them.
If you wish for your practice to become a single, unified whole, you will not achieve it even after many years.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one must not seek after words or follow along with phrases, nor record sayings and utterances;
for this not only provides no benefit but creates obstacles to one's practice. It turns genuine practice, on the contrary, into mere discursive thought.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one most fears intellectual speculation (*vikalpa*). To force the mind to settle upon an object is to distance oneself further from the Way;

even if one were to wait until Maitreya’s descent, it would surely remain irrelevant. However, for those who have truly given rise to the great doubt, it fills all of space such that they are unaware of the very name "space.
It is as if they are sitting amidst silver mountains and iron walls, desiring only to attain [realization].
This is the way to live. If you do not find this way to live, how can you attain peace and stability? Simply proceed in this manner;
when the time arrives, success will come naturally.
Recently, there have been certain heterodox teachers who instruct people not to apply effort toward the "going beyond" (wu-gong), but rather to apply effort toward the "preparatory work" (gong-fu).
They further claim that the ancients never engaged in such preparatory work. These words are most poisonous; they delude and mislead later students, leading them into hell.
Chan Master Dayi’s *Sitting Meditation Inscription* says: "By all means do not say that the Way does not require study;
the ancient sages strove diligently as a guiding compass. Although it is the empty ground of an old pavilion, to win it back even once is difficult.

If one claims that there is no need for investigation and study, asserting that the principle has already been attained, such a person is a "Maitreya born by nature" or a "Śākyamuni by default. These types of people—

They are called "those who deserve pity. This is because they do not engage in personal investigation. Upon seeing an ancient master’s single question and answer, they immediately claim to have attained realization;
they then take it upon themselves to interpret it through their own intellectual consciousness and deceive others with it.
Or, when they suddenly contract a severe fever and their cries of agony reach the heavens, everything they had spent their lives interpreting proves useless. Or, when the moment of death arrives...
At the moment of death, one is like a crab falling into a boiling cauldron; hands flail and feet scramble in confusion—what use is regret then?
Master Huangbo said: "When worldly toil is utterly cast off, the matter is extraordinary; grasp the rope-head tightly and perform this scene."
"Unless one’s bones are thoroughly chilled by the cold, how can one obtain the fragrance of plum blossoms that strikes the nose? These words are most intimate.
If you use this verse to exhort yourself at all times in your practice, you will naturally succeed.
It is like a journey of a hundred *li*: for every step taken, one draws closer; if you do not walk, you remain right here. Even if you can speak of the destination...
Worldly affairs may be thoroughly understood and clearly mastered, yet one will ultimately never arrive home; what significant matter could such achievements possibly accomplish?
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one most fears intellectual deliberation—such as composing poetry, gāthās, or prose essays.
If one’s poems and gāthās are perfected, one is called a poet; if one’s prose and essays are skillful, one is termed a scholar. These have no connection whatsoever with the study of Chan.
Regarding the practice of the Buddha-Dharma: whenever one encounters circumstances—whether favorable or adverse—that stir the mind’s perceptions, one must immediately awaken to them.
One should then seize the *huatou* (critical phrase) and not allow oneself to be turned by external conditions; only then can progress be achieved.
Some say that failing to hold fast to these three words is a way of misleading people; students must examine this carefully.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, if the state of doubt (*samsaya*) is not resolved, it is like standing on the brink of a deep abyss or treading upon thin ice.
To lose mindfulness for even a hair’s breadth is to lose one’s body and life. Because this doubt is not resolved, the Great Principle remains unclarified.

When the single breath does not return, it is another lifetime; led by the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one cannot avoid departing with the karmic consciousness, undergoing a change of head and face.
One is neither aware nor cognizant of it. Because of this, doubt arises regarding what is above; furthermore, another layer of doubt is added. One must seize the *huatou* (critical phrase):
if it is not clear, one must resolutely strive for clarity; if it is not broken through, one must resolutely strive for its breakthrough. It is like catching a thief: one must see the stolen goods.
The practice of the Buddha-dharma must be diligent, correct, continuous, and expansive. What is meant by diligence? Human life hangs by a thread;
until the Great Matter is clarified, one breath may not remain, and the path ahead will be vast and uncertain—knowing not where one shall go.
One cannot but be diligent. An ancient worthy said: "It is like a hemp rope soaking in water; with every step, it becomes tighter and tighter. What is meant by "correct"?
A student must possess the eye that discerns the Dharma (*dharmavicaya-cakṣus*). Among the three thousand seven hundred patriarchs, there are many exemplary models.
If there is an error of even a hair’s breadth, one enters a deviant path. As the Sūtra says: "This alone is the one reality; all else is but fabrication."
True. What is meant by "dense and continuous"? The eyebrows are joined with empty space; a needle cannot pierce them, water cannot moisten them; not even a hair’s breadth of gap is permitted.
If there were a gap of even a hair’s breadth, then the realm of demons would seize that opening to enter.
As an ancient worthy said: "If for a single moment one is not present, it is the same as being a dead person. What is meant by "fused and open"? The world...
One zhang wide. If the ancient mirror is one zhang wide, then the hearth is one zhang wide.
It must not be grasped and held in one place, nor caught firmly by the head of a dead snake, nor tied and dropped at both ends.
Vast and expansive. As the Ancient Sage said: "Perfectly identical to the great void, without deficiency and without excess. This is truly arriving.
In the state of vast openness and dissolution, one does not perceive body or mind within, nor does one perceive the world without;
only then does one find the path of entry. These four stages are not sequential layers; they must be attained simultaneously.
If one is tense but does not give rise [to realization], then one is laboring in vain. If one is correct but not tense, then one cannot enter.
Once entered, it must be continuous and subtle before it can be in accord. Once in accord, it must be fused and expansive before it becomes the realm of transformation.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, not even a hair’s breadth of extraneous thought can be permitted.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one must single-mindedly maintain the original koan, giving rise to a state of doubt and striving with fierce resolve to reach its ultimate resolution.

If there is even the slightest extraneous thought, as the ancients said, it is like "poisonous filth entering the heart"; this will not only harm one's physical life, but will also injure one's wisdom.
Scholars must be careful regarding this matter of "separate mindfulness.
What I mean by "separate mindfulness" applies not only to worldly dharmas; within the Buddha-dharma, everything other than the investigation of the mind is termed "separate mindfulness.
Furthermore, this applies not only to matters within the Buddha-dharma, but even to grasping at characteristics upon the substance of the mind itself.
To abandon them, to let go of them, to grasp them, and to transform them— all these are distinct modes of thought.
The practice of the Buddha-dharma consists in casting aside all worldly phenomena— whatever objects may be lovable or hateful,
whatever emotions may be joyful or sorrowful— and retaining only one's own right awakening, disregarding everything else.
Furthermore, one must become a person of no utility. Let him come to defeat me;
I shall simply remain ignorant and indifferent. Let him come to mock me; I shall simply remain ignorant and indifferent.
I shall attend only to my own right awakening, never flagging for a moment.
Regarding the practice of the Buddha-dharma, many who attempt it say they cannot succeed. Yet, precisely because one cannot succeed, one must simply continue to practice.
It is like a person who does not know the way: they must simply set out to find it. One cannot say that because they fail to find the way, they should give up.
It is like one who has found the path: what matters is walking. One must go straight until reaching home;
one must not linger on the road without moving forward. Otherwise, there will never be a day when one arrives home.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, the most feared thing is a clever mind. A clever mind is a strict contraindication;

if it is offended by even a hair’s breadth, then even if the true medicine appears before one, it cannot save them. If one is truly a person of inquiry, their eyes are like those of the blind and their ears like those of the deaf;
as soon as a thought arises, it is as if they have run headlong into a silver mountain and an iron wall.
In this way, one's practice will finally achieve resonance.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one does not fear making mistakes; one only fears not recognizing them as such.

Even if one happens to walk upon an erroneous path, if one is willing to recognize that error in a single thought-moment, this is the very foundation for becoming a Buddha or a Patriarch, and the essential highway for transcending birth and death.
It is also the sharp weapon for tearing through the net of Māra. Śākyamuni Buddha verified each and every point regarding the teachings of the non-Buddhists;

he simply did not sit within their conceptual traps. One should know that by means of the four characters "abandon what is erroneous," one proceeds from the stage of an ordinary person all the way to the rank of Buddhahood.
This principle applies not only to the supramundane Dharma, but even within the mundane world, when there is a lapse in mindfulness—only...
If one eliminates a single instance of knowing one's error and abandons it, one can immediately become a pure and virtuous person.
However, if one stubbornly clings to one's mistakes as being right and refuses to acknowledge them, then even if a living Buddha were to appear before them, they could not be saved.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one must not avoid clamor to seek stillness, nor close the eyes and sit within a "ghost cave" to conduct one's business.
As the ancients said: "Sitting beneath a black mountain, soaked in dead water—what can this possibly accomplish?
One must simply be able to work within the conditions of sensory objects; this is precisely where true efficacy is found. A single phrase of the *huatou* should be placed directly before you.

Whether upon the eyebrows and eyelashes, while walking or sitting, while putting on clothes and eating meals, or while welcoming guests and attending to visitors—one must simply clarify where this single phrase-head falls.
One day, while washing one's face, one touches the bridge of one’s own nose;
realizing it was all along right there before one, one attains a state of effortless ease. This is truly "attaining it" without expending any effort at all.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, one most fears taking the conscious spirit as the work of the Buddha.

Whether it be raising an eyebrow, blinking an eye, shaking the head, or turning the brain about, to think there is anything particularly marvelous therein—if you take this conscious spirit as the true reality, you will undoubtedly enter the ranks of the non-Buddhists.
Truly, you have taken the wrong path. It is a great pity.
The practice of the Buddha-dharma requires focusing one's mind on a single koan; one must not seek intellectual understanding through all the koans.
Even if one can understand them, it remains merely an intellectual comprehension and is not realization (*wu*). As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "This Dharma..."
It cannot be reached through discursive thought or conceptual discrimination. As the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states:

"To take thought as the mind and attempt to fathom the realm of the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment is like trying to heat Mount Sumeru with a firefly’s glow; one will ultimately never succeed. Dongshan said:

"To attempt to study the profound mystery with the conscious mind is much like heading west while actually facing east. Generally speaking, such forced interpretation is mere intellectual fabrication.
Regarding public cases (kōan): one must have blood beneath the skin and recognize a sense of shame before they can be mastered.
In the practice of the Buddha-dharma, the greatest fear is falling into emptiness. When the critical phrase (hwadu) is present before you, how could there be any room for emptiness?
Yet, even this very fear of falling into emptiness prevents one from becoming empty; how much more so when the words of the case are manifest before you?

In the secret transmission of the general purport of the Buddha-dharma, it is said that the Śākya renounced his home to study the Way; critics debate this, claiming he disregarded the principles of human relations (*lunji*). Yet they fail to realize that he never truly renounced them.
Take, for instance, the person of Śākyamuni himself: first he delivered his father, King Śuddhodana, and his mother, Queen Māyā; next, he delivered Yaśodharā...

[The Buddha] bestowed [the precepts] upon Śūdra, then upon Rāhula, and then upon Ānanda. These relationships—of ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife, and elder and younger brother—have not been abandoned at all.
How, then, can it be said that the social order has been cast aside? Even if one were to claim it has been discarded, this argument was initiated by the bhikṣus;
as for officials, lay devotees, and white-robed householders, none of them are separated from their sovereign or their parents. And yet, they all...
One may study the Way and cultivate reality; who then could find grounds to dismiss such a person on account of their social relations?

Suppose there were a Buddhist who did not understand the human condition, knowing only how to greedily nourish his own belly, without considering the observance of the fast or the precept against killing.

He values humans while degrading other beings, slaughtering the multitudes of living spirits as if they were merely melons or gourds. He fails to realize that animals and strange species are all equally sentient beings, all possessing—

It is the Buddha-nature. To use gauze and brocade as floral ornaments, unaware that one is killing the lives of ten thousand silkworms and burning away the splendor of their floating bodies—this is a pity.

To take delicacies of a hundred flavors as savory fare, unaware that one is boiling the fresh creatures of land and water and clogging the pores of the hungry stomachs—this is a great sin. Hawks, dogs, poisoned arrows, and spears fill the mountain forests.

Nets and snares fill the rivers and seas; oxen, sheep, pigs, and deer lie scattered in abundance throughout the markets and capitals. Fish, turtles, shrimp, and crabs leave a stench of filth upon the streets.
Having grown accustomed to these practices, they remain complacent and feel no dread, unaware that they are binding themselves in karmic resentment and debt.
Retribution is inexhaustible. With pure songs and exquisite dances, flutes and strings played in harmony, women are cherished and men rejoice; their hearts are satisfied and their minds entertained.
The eminent, the wise, the heroic, and the outstanding regard this as something within their natural domain, unaware that it is the very root of their downfall into the boundless ocean of desire.
Meeting with a favorable age and opportune times, they vie for fame and compete for profit; they bring glory to their neighborhoods and inspire envy on the roads. Within—
Those above this level generally all "dip their fingers" [into the pot], failing to realize that the root of samsaric wandering lies in illusions and bubbles, which are impermanent.

Bound by emotional attachments and greedily clinging to their own kin, their minds are entangled with suffering and pleasure, and their thoughts are fettered by birth and death; they do not know there is liberation.
They falsely distinguish between self and others, laboring to cultivate favor and resentment; they do not know there is equality. Let us cease our discussion for now.

At present, (this is a great error). How could it be that one does not know the cause and effect of good and evil after death? Even after passing through a thousand births and ten thousand kalpas, the retribution will not be exhausted.

(Many who do not understand must come to know. From the time the Buddha-dharma became clearly manifest, all has been fully understood. Although there are many who continue to commit various transgressions as before, those who receive the teachings and practice them are likewise not few.
That they serve as a bridge and raft for the world’s way—how great this is! Confucianism...
Worldly dharmas are used to govern social teachings and to preserve and gather one’s legacy during life.
Buddhist dharmas are for transcending the world, used to cultivate the spiritual nature and to ascend to higher realms after death. Originally, these two do not harm one another;
why prevent their coexistence?
People say that the study of the Buddha-dharma seeks the mind with the mind; this is to employ the mind by means of the mind.

It appears as if there were two minds, yet they do not realize that the mind is one: profound stillness and spiritual luminosity, perfectly interfused and unimpeded, encompassing all phenomena and containing the ten directions.
Most intelligent and most wondrous, the mind is simply one; it is not twofold. Because it is perfectly interfused...
Unimpeded, one externally contemplates the hundred things; it is simply this single mind. Internally contemplating the single mind is also simply this single mind.
External contemplation of the hundred things is called "emitting light"; internal contemplation of the single mind is called "reflective illumination.
That this mind can both emit light and reflect illumination is why it is so spiritual and wondrous. The moon can illuminate the myriad things.
A mirror cannot reflect back upon itself; though it can reflect the myriad phenomena, it likewise lacks the capacity for self-reflection because the luminosity of both is devoid of sentience.
The mind can observe all things and can also reflect back upon its own spirit; this is sentience.
Whether the mind is defiled or pure, whether it is sagely or ordinary—the mind knows this of itself. This is precisely what is meant by "using the mind to observe the mind."
It does not mean that the object of observation is one mind while the observer is another mind.

Since the mind can already observe the hundred things externally, how could it not be able to observe the one mind internally? Therefore, the functions of the ears and eyes can focus on one thing but not two;
that which takes the one as one is the physical form. The mind, however, can be one and can be myriad; that which takes the myriad as [one] is the spirit.
The first is the spirit (*shen*). Thus, the mind is able to observe the mind. Now, one desires the mind to be pure; by removing defilement, purity is attained.
Who could act as the "mind" for this mind? It is acceptable to say that one observes the mind with the mind, and it is also acceptable to say that one seeks the mind with the mind.
However, it is not permissible to say that one uses the mind with the mind. If one were to observe the mind with the mind...
To claim that there are two minds—that one mind perceives the hundred things and thus constitutes a hundred minds—is a great error.
The commentators say: "In the study of the Śākya [Buddhists], they possess 'reverence which makes the internal straight,' but they lack 'righteousness which makes the external square.'"
I have not heard of such a thing. Now, as for saying that the Buddha’s reverence consists in rectifying the inner self: this is correct.

For the Buddha’s inner mind employs *śamatha* (calm abiding) solely to cut off the scattering of dust; this is called "quiescence" (*jiji*). It employs *vipaśyanā* (insight observation) to eliminate darkness and obscurity;

this is called "alertness" (*xingxing*). When one abides while constantly observing, this abiding is not a state of neutral indifference (*avyākṛta*). When one observes while constantly abiding, this observation is not a state of distracted conceptualization. Such concentration is like the great earth.
Unmoved by the winds of the eight worldly concerns, wisdom is like the bright moon, illuminating all things without exception.

Taking wisdom as concentration, the essence of concentration is profoundly still; taking concentration as wisdom, the function of wisdom is tranquil and silent. Thus, cessation and contemplation serve as the cause.

Concentration and wisdom constitute its function, while merit is preceded by the precepts. To strictly purify the *vinaya* and to maintain reverence so as to rectify the inner self may be called truly harmonizing with the teachings of Confucianism.

However, one must ensure that both body and mind are reverent, such that practice and understanding correspond; internally cultivating contemplative wisdom and externally solemnizing one’s deportment;
performing the *poṣadha* and *karma* according to the Tathāgata’s bequeathed rules; and making the six perfections and myriad practices one's own for the sake of Buddhahood.
Regarding the adornment of practice: In speech, one must not kill; even the harming of a flying insect or a crawling worm constitutes killing.

In speech, one must not steal; even the scent of incense wafting from the nostrils constitutes stealing. In speech, one must not engage in lust; even hearing the sound of hairpins and bracelets through a wall constitutes lust.
In speech, one must not covet; thus, one dares not covet even a single blade of grass or a single needle. In speech, one must not harbor anger; thus, as for the limbs and body—
Torn and rent, yet one dares not harbor anger. Speech that is not deluded belongs to the Samyaksambuddha Tathāgata;
yet, as long as even a single grade of ignorance remains unbroken, one is still subject to delusion. In principle, this extends beyond the mundane world and may be called both solemn and profound.

Those who remain stagnant and enter a state of withered desiccation are merely Pratyekabuddhas of the Hīnayāna, not those of the Mahāyāna’s Perfect and Sudden gate. It is through thorough penetration that one returns to the source.
As for those who act with license, they are but those given to dissipation and wild meditation, violating the Vinaya of the Brahma Net and the Prātimokṣa;

the fault lies with the student. What harm does this do to the Buddha? Such is the Buddha’s solemn and majestic standard. All of this has been transmitted from the Golden Mouth and recorded in the Pearl-Shell Scriptures;
it is clear and manifest. How can it be said that these are not the fundamental principles of instruction?
The proponent says: The Confucian pursuit of recovering the scattered mind resembles the Buddhist description of entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
However, at this point, the Buddhist [view] is as if the mind has died and lacks a sovereign master. This statement seems plausible but is actually incorrect. As for "recovering the scattered mind":
The mind races across thousands of miles; it cannot withstand its flickering and chaotic flight. Even if one seeks to restrain it, there may not yet be a handle to grasp.
To settle the mind is to collect it in a single point, so that it becomes naturally concentrated, tranquil, and serene.
By waiting patiently, wisdom-light will spontaneously arise. To call the settled mind "death" is not to understand meditative concentration (samādhi). — The Buddha.
When the Master’s words ceased, he continued: "If one speaks of stillness, one must simultaneously observe; if one speaks of silence, one must simultaneously illuminate.
There is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, wherein not a single dharma is established; there is the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*, wherein the myriad dharmas stand in dense array.

It is like a single orb of the moon that illuminates ten thousand waves, yet each wave possesses its own moon, while the moon remains but a single orb. It is like a rain of a single flavor that causes all things to flourish."

The myriad things. Each of these myriad things receives its own rain, yet that rain is of a single flavor. When it manifests in the heavens, there arise the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, all composed of fragrant flowers and jeweled terraces.
When it manifests in hell, there arise the copper pillars and iron beds, yet they are woven together into a Flower Treasury (Kusuma-garbha).
Human kings, ministers, and manifested Bodhisattvas appear; even snails, shells, and clams are the transformed bodies of Great Beings (Mahāsattva). Such are the seeds.
The various functions and diverse affairs all arise from within stillness and concentration. Can it be said that this is what is meant by the "extinction of the mind"?
Commentators maintain that what the Buddha calls "nature" (prakṛti) is precisely what the sages call "mind" (citta); and what the Buddha calls "mind" is precisely what the sages... [call nature].
Regarding what is called "mind" (*manas*): the Buddha originally did not recognize this as the principle (*li*).
Instead, he identified cognition, sensation, movement, the capacity to see, hear, think, and act as being the principle. This statement is a great error.
According to the Buddha’s teaching, the nature of mind (*cittatā*) is originally a single entity—a singular, pure, vast, wondrously profound, and perfectly luminous reality within heaven and earth.
This is called "nature" (*xing*). That which is the numinous penetration of nature is called "mind" (*xin*). Nature is like the brightness of a mirror; mind is like the reflecting of the mirror.
In reality, they are one and the same thing. That which encompasses everything without exception is collectively termed "nature.
When that nature is numinously penetrating, it is termed "mind. Thus, from mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, tiles, and pebbles, all possess nature.
Only that which possesses the human nature capable of spiritual intelligence, cognition, and awareness can be called "mind" (*citta*).
Mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, tiles, and pebbles are merely termed "nature" (*prakṛti*); they are not termed "mind.

That which the Buddha calls "mind" is pure, vast, wondrously profound, and perfectly luminous; it is termed "original enlightenment" (*mūla-bodhi*), termed "prajñā," and termed the "Vairocana-nature-ocean."
This is called the "Muni's Jewel. That which is referred to as "mind" (yi) is the consciousness-spirit (shishen) of the human heart, the very root of birth and death.
It is for this reason that the Buddha, through his perfect cultivation and wondrous awakening, necessarily transforms this consciousness-spirit into wisdom.
This is what is meant by "transforming the ordinary person into a sage. For both the ordinary person and the sage fundamentally possess this same mind-nature.
Because the ordinary person is deluded regarding the truth and pursues the false, their wisdom is transformed into the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*).
Because the sage shatters the false and returns to the true, their consciousness-spirit is transformed into wisdom. This [consciousness-spirit] is precisely that which the Buddha rebuked. It is...
It is said: What the Buddha calls "mind" (citta) is precisely what the sages call "intention" (manas). There have been many errors in their terminology.

When one returns to the truth according to the Buddhist teaching, then cognition, movement, seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting—being able to see, hear, speak, and act—is none other than this nature (prakṛti).
When ordinary people pursue delusion, then cognition, movement, seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting—being able to see... [and so forth].
Hearing, being able to speak, and being able to move—all these are nothing but delusions.

To claim that the Buddhists recognize only that which is capable of seeing, hearing, speaking, and moving as being "nature" (xing)—is one not foolish? Indeed, it cannot be denied that the capacity to see, hear, speak, and move constitutes nature;
yet to say that this is what the Buddhists mean by "pure, vast, wondrously profound, and perfectly luminous"—[is surely a misunderstanding].

"Nature" (xing) is named solely in relation to seeing, hearing, speaking, and acting; does such a principle exist? Now, when speaking of nature, the Tathāgata unifies the single nature within the source of all things.
When speaking of principle (li), the Tathāgata elucidates the myriad principles within phenomena and affairs.

As for the vastness of principle, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm horizontally; as for the subtlety of principle, it penetrates into the finest hair-tip vertically. This is the shattering of views by the Two Vehicles.

To contemplate [the principle] while its investigation of reality remains coarse is the way of a Bodhisattva breaking through ignorance; yet even for a Bodhisattva, the investigation of reality reaches its utmost refinement.
If even one grade of ignorance remains unbroken in the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), then the principle still possesses obstructions.

Only upon entering the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) does the single truth become thoroughly penetrated and the ten thousand miles become transparently clear. To say that one does not recognize the word "principle" (*li*)—what kind of statement is that? For principle has its own...
However, when there is deliberate arrangement, one is already far removed from the truth; for while principles each have their proper place, to force them into a convergence is to deviate from them.
That which exists without being arranged, and that which accords without being converged upon—this is the ultimate subtlety of Buddhist principle.
This is the transformation of white wisdom, yet it functions as the consciousness-spirit (*vijñāna*). The more one’s intellectual vision increases, the more one’s essential nature becomes obscured.

Though they may claim their discourse on principles is clear and their language is subtle, these are entirely the livelihood of ghosts—manipulating the vital spirit while remaining unaware that one must sever all names and words and sweep away all conceptual meanings. They take all the habitual patterns and conceptual frameworks of their ordinary lives and...

Suddenly overturning everything completely, there is a state of intermediate cessation and awakening. Through the cultivation of *prajñā* and contemplation, one becomes profoundly still yet vividly alert.

Suddenly, like a flash of lightning, the lotus flower blooms for the first time; this is called "Great Enlightenment. This is truly because the *huatou* (critical phrase) of the Chan school is perfectly wondrous;
it possesses no inherent flavor or meaning, allowing one to abandon conceptual discrimination and attain sovereignty, thereby transforming the consciousness-essence.
This constitutes the perfection of Prajñā. One must understand that the Sixth Patriarch was a woodcutter; though he could not recognize a single character, he immediately attained realization.
Ānanda was a man of vast learning and perfect retention; only after exhausting his extensive knowledge did he awaken to the true emptiness.
There is indeed a profound reason for this.
The treatise says: "The Buddha recognizes only the human mind; there is no so-called 'mind of the Way' (daoxin).
One does not realize that what the Buddha most censures is the human mind, and what he most cultivates is the mind of the Way. When there is good and no evil, this is the mind of the Buddha’s Way;
thus, all evils are utterly eliminated and all myriad virtues converge. When there is purity and no defilement, this is the mind of the Buddha’s Way; thus, even a single speck of dust—"

It is unstained; its myriad virtues are perfectly pure. Possessing both essence and function, this is the Way and the Buddha-mind. Thus, it is quiescent yet ever-illuminating, and illuminating yet ever-quiescent.
It takes the non-abiding of nature and characteristics as its principle, and the non-obstruction of phenomena and principle as its standard.
The Buddha is entirely awakening, and awakening is entirely the Way—even down to the human mind, which is termed the "conscious spirit" (*vijñāna*) and is termed a defiled dharma.
The six sense organs are used in delusion, and the eight consciousnesses burn fiercely; these are the root causes of birth and death and the seeds for the three miserable realms.

It is precisely for the sake of eliminating these that the Buddha diligently practices. To say that the Buddha merely recognizes the human mind—how could one know whether such a person is truly a Buddha?
The Buddha says "non-thought" (amanasikāra); this refers to the absence of deluded thoughts, wherein right mindfulness is not extinguished, for the wisdom of *prajñā* remains present.
The non-Buddhists speak of "thoughtlessness" (asaṃjñā); therein right mindfulness is extinguished, as there is no permeation by the contemplation of the wisdom of *prajñā*.
Question: It is said that concentration (*samādhi*) can give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*); can wisdom also give rise to concentration? Answer:

The arising of concentration from wisdom is even swifter than the arising of wisdom from concentration. When concentration gives rise to wisdom, it is like water that, once settled, reflects all things without ceasing.

When wisdom gives rise to concentration, it is like a lamp of wisdom that, with a single flash of brilliance, extinguishes all shadows and strange apparitions. Miaoxi said: "People say that one must first achieve stillness before one attains awakening."
I attained awakening and only then became still. Before awakening, my mind and consciousness were scattered and flying about; once awakened, they settled into a state of profound composure.

When asked, "Are insentient things Buddhas? I replied, "Insentient things are Buddhas. Then [the questioner] said, "In that case, dead people must be Tathāgatas. To which I replied, "So-called 'no'..."
Sentiment is not the absence of ordinary sentiment; it is not the absence of noble sentiment. Question: What is called noble sentiment? What is called ordinary sentiment? Answer:
To be without discrimination between right and wrong, and regarding all objects and phenomena, neither to cling nor to grasp—this is called noble sentiment.
To possess discrimination between right and wrong, and to grasp and cling to all objects—this is called ordinary sentiment. There is no...
Ordinary sentiment and holy sentiment—sentiment is also non-sentiment.
*The Direct Pointing of the Chan School* (End).
